messages.subject: Box plot based dashboard.
messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

I am trying to create a dashboard report using ggplot2. My goal is to have something similar to this (follow here for macro picture <http://blog.helpingadvisors.com/wp-content/uploads/2014/12/Asset-Class-Dashboard-2014.jpg>):

 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-ILx36qI15U0/VKkKU4uiBwI/AAAAAAAAAAg/3yWIlu9PG_c/s1600/Asset-Class-Dashboard-2014.jpg>

The input is historical data for multiple variable.
Grey area marks the range, Blue 1 standard deviation from the mean (in general boxplot, jost styled differently)

Yellow arrow marks the most recent value.

Any ideas on the most efficient way to go with it?

At the moment i have two datasets:
1. Dataset with historical values for each variable
2. Summary dataset for each variable (with min, max, mean, SD, and last vale extracted)

Thanks in advance.
To

To,

Since you have min and max values and can compute on the fly the SD min/max values you could use multiple layers of geom_bar and then perhaps a dot for the current value. Putting all of the values on the chart could probably be done with geom_text, but it likely won't look at pretty without some serious tuning/modifications.

Supply your summary dataset and perhaps someone can get you started.

Brandon

messages.body_plain:
Thank you guys for recommendations my attempt worked out perfectly (see code bellow), however I ran into other problem that is I beleive related with the way Ggplot2 handles data:

I run this function to generate graph for each variable:
DashPlot <- function(Name, Mean, SD, Min, Max, Last){
    R1 <- Mean - SD
    R2 <- Mean + SD
    Range <- Max-Min
    Plot <- ggplot() +
        geom_rect(mapping=aes(xmin=Min, xmax=Max, ymin=0, ymax=1.4), fill="lightblue")
    list(is.numeric(Min), Plot)
}

DashPlot("U.S. Treasury note 10 Year Yield", 6.47, 2.38, 1.46, 15.48, 2.19)

While function works, if I have variables Name, Mean, SD, Min, Max, Last defined in the global environment, it seems not to find it if I attempt to submit values through the function.
Any ideas why it can be the case?

[[1]]
[1] TRUE

[[2]]
Error in eval(expr, envir, enclos) : object 'Min' not found

For those who might be interested in design problem, successful dashboard plot and code are here:

 <https://lh5.googleusercontent.com/-CG18EbyG2og/VKvMCaDY3FI/AAAAAAAAABA/1ZNStUGmCI0/s1600/U.S.%2BTreasury%2Bnote%2B10%2BYear%2BYield%2B.jpeg>

Plot <- ggplot() +
    geom_rect(mapping=aes(xmin=Min, xmax=Max, ymin=0, ymax=1.4), fill="white") +
    geom_rect(mapping=aes(xmin=Min, xmax=Max, ymin=0, ymax=1), fill="#DCDCDC") +
    geom_rect(mapping=aes(xmin=R1, xmax=R2, ymin=0, ymax=1), fill="#7EC0EE") +
    geom_point(mapping=aes(x=Last, y=1), colour="orange", size=5, shape=18) +
    geom_rect(mapping=aes(xmin=Last-Range/20, xmax=Last+Range/20, ymin=1, ymax=1.4), fill="orange") +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks=sort(c(Min,R1,R2,Max))) +
    scale_y_continuous(breaks=NULL) +
    xlab(paste(Name)) + ylab("")

Plot <- Plot + theme(panel.background = element_rect(fill = "white"),
                         legend.position="none",
                         axis.text.x = element_text(size = 9),

Plot <- Plot + annotate("text", label = paste(Last), x = Last, y = 1.2, size = 3, colour = "white")+

Calls within aes() are mapped to variables. This is what's happening with your fill variable. You have a factor (label) that has two levels (matched and unmatched). These variables are mapped to blue and pink and displayed.

You can supply a single value to the alpha in either the geom_() or aes() and you get the same result. (I thought I previously tried in aes() and failed, but my history says otherwise).
ggplot(testframe, aes(age, fill = label, alpha = 0.2)) + geom_density (pos="dodge")

ggplot(testframe, aes(age, fill = label)) + geom_density (alpha = 0.2, pos="dodge")

When you add I() to the mix, I'm not actually sure what it's doing. According to ?I():

Function I has two main uses.
In function data.frame. Protecting an object by enclosing it in I() in a call to data.frame inhibits the conversion of character vectors to factors and the dropping of names, and ensures that matrices are inserted as single columns. I can also be used to protect objects which are to be added to a data frame, or converted to a data frame via as.data.frame.
It achieves this by prepending the class "AsIs" to the object's classes. Class "AsIs" has a few of its own methods, including for [, as.data.frame, print and format.
In function formula. There it is used to inhibit the interpretation of operators such as "+", "-", "*" and "^" as formula operators, so they are used as arithmetical operators. This is interpreted as a symbol by terms.formula.
The error it gives is as though it is only trying to change the alpha of a single row in your data.frame. This obviously wouldn't work, but if you make it long enough it does.

I'm responding to Brandon's post but the message is actually directed at the OP.

In ggplot2, I() is used to set the value of an aesthetic in qplot(). The idiom does not extend to ggplot() AFAIK. This is one reason why (IMO), when learning ggplot2,
one should stick to either qplot() or ggplot() while learning the package. Once the principles are understood, it's easier to jump back and forth between them without being confused by their syntactic differences. I tend to use ggplot() almost exclusively, but that's my choice - many people use both interchangeably with great success.

If you map an aesthetic to a single value inside aes(), it will produce a legend with that single value rendered. ggplot2 renders legends for aesthetics that are mapped - either to variables (preferred) or single values (usually unwanted, but not always). [There are a couple of exceptions to the rule about mapped variables automatically producing legends, but they are not relevant to your present example.]

But that's really inelegant and I feel like ggplot probably has some function that I'm overlooking.  I've tried various permutations of ..count.., but no matter what I do, if I try to attack it without summarizing the data outside of ggplot first, it fails.

Anyway, any guidance on this matter would be helpful!

Thanks,
Danielle

Hi Tian,

I recreate your problem with a little bit of made-up data:

x1 <- 1:20
y1 <- x1+0.5
x2 <- x1+rnorm(20,sd=0.01)
y2 <- 2*x2+0.5

d <- data.frame(x1,y1,x2,y2)

What you need is to have the colour and shape mapped to a variable
identifying the pair of columns that it came from (point1, point2...
in your email). So if you set up your data along these lines
(that is, "long" rather than "wide" - package reshape2 can probably
help here if you have a lot of columns to deal with):

dd<-data.frame(x=c(x1,x2),y=c(y1,y2),f=rep(c("p1","p2"),each=20))

and map colour and shape to f within an aes when plotting, then

ggplot(dd,aes(x=x,y=y))+geom_point(aes(colour=f,shape=f))

should get you started.

Ron.

The trim argument's description implies that it only changes the end positions of the density. However, for some data, it also draws a vertical line through the entire density area. This is undesirable.

The bandwidth adjustment parameter causes more strangeness, with a wedge placed in the middle of the violin.

plot <- ggplot(plotData, aes(x = analysis, y = overlap)) + geom_violin(trim = FALSE, adjust = 2) + scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 100))
plot    # Strange wedge.

messages.subject: Divide Legend into Two Columns, Each with Its Own Title
messages.subject_clean: Divide Legend into Two Columns, Each with Its Own Title
messages.body_plain:
I recently worked on a Stack Overflow question <http://stackoverflow.com/questions/27803710/ggplot2-divide-legend-into-two-columns-each-with-its-own-title/27804153#27804153> in which the poster wanted to have the legend in two columns, controlling which factor levels were in each column, and also putting a separate legend title over each column. I was able to get a custom split of the factor levels by adding a dummy factor level. However, I had two issues in trying to create separate legend titles. First, I had to resort to grob manipulation, which worked, but which required a lot of extra code and trial and error placement of the grobs. Second, even though I turned off clipping for all pre-existing grobs, the titles I created with the text grobs are still clipped by the pre-existing legend grob.

So, my questions are:
1) Is there a way to do this within ggplot2, without having to resort to grobs manipulation?
2) If not, is there an easier way to create and position the text grobs for the custom legend titles?
3) Why is the legend still clipping the text grobs and how can I fix this so that the text grobs are "on top" of the legend grob?

Please feel free to post an answer on Stack Overflow in addition to any response you provide here. Alternatively, I'll be happy to add any responses I receive here to my SO answer, <http://stackoverflow.com/questions/27803710/ggplot2-divide-legend-into-two-columns-each-with-its-own-title/27804153#27804153> with credit of course.

Here's the code for the plot, using the diamonds data frame:
library(gtable)

# Add dummy factor level to achieve desired column split in legend
diamonds$cut = factor(diamonds$cut, levels=c("Fair", "Good", " ", "Very Good",
                                             "Premium", "Ideal"))

# Initial plot with two-column legend and extra margin space between plot area and legend where we'll place
# the two custom legend titles
p = ggplot(diamonds, aes(color, fill=cut)) + geom_bar() +
  scale_fill_manual(values=c(hcl(seq(15,325,length.out=5), 100, 65)[1:2],
                             "white",
                             hcl(seq(15,325,length.out=5), 100, 65)[3:5]),
                    drop=FALSE) +
  guides(fill=guide_legend(ncol=2)) +
  theme(legend.position=c(0.5,-0.26),
        plot.margin=unit(c(1,1,7,1),"lines")) +
  labs(fill="")

# Add two text grobs
p = p + annotation_custom(
    grob = textGrob(label = "First\nGroup",
                    hjust = 0.5, gp = gpar(cex = 0.7)),
    ymin = -2200, ymax = -2200, xmin = 3.45, xmax = 3.45) +
  annotation_custom(
    grob = textGrob(label = "Second\nGroup",
                    hjust = 0.5, gp = gpar(cex = 0.7)),
    ymin = -2200, ymax = -2200, xmin = 4.2, xmax = 4.2)

# Override clipping and draw plot
gt <- ggplot_gtable(ggplot_build(p))
gt$layout$clip <- "off"
grid.draw(gt)

Thanks,
Joel

messages.body_plain:
The data for the plot can be extracted, but it might be easier to pre-summarise the data yourself. Here are examples of both methods, using the built-in mtcars data frame for illustration:

library(gridExtra) # For grid.arrange function
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr) # For summarizing data

Method 1: Use ggplot_build to extract data from plot object.

# Create a plot similar to yours
p1 = ggplot(mtcars, aes(x=mpg, y=..density.., fill=factor(cyl))) + geom_histogram(binwidth=5)

# Extract data using function ggplot_build
p1build = ggplot_build(p1)
plotData = p1build$data[[1]]

Where plotData is a data frame containing the data that ggplot created to build the histogram. One more thing: I don't think you need "y=..density..".

Method 2: Pre-summarize the data

# Pre-summarize the data
mpgBins = mtcars %>% group_by(cyl, mpgCut=cut(mpg, seq(0,40,5))) %>%
  summarise(count=n())

You can also, of course, plot the pre-summarized data:

p2 = ggplot(mpgBins, aes(mpgCut, count, fill=factor(cyl))) +
  geom_bar(stat="identity")

# Compare the two plots
grid.arrange(p1,p2)

If you want to add the categorical bins to your original data set, rather than just have a summary version, you can use the cut function for that as well:

mtcars = mtcars %>%
                  mutate(mpgBins = cut(mpg, seq(0, 40, 5)))

or, in base R

mtcars$mpgBins = cut(mtcars$mpgBins, seq(0, 40, 5))

Hope that helps.

Joel

I will echo the comments of some on doing this though, in that it's generally a bad idea if you expect your code to be portable.

Brandon

messages.subject: Re: barplot - fixed width of bars
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

Here are a couple of suggestions. I think the first is what you were after.

library(ggplot2)
ggplot(dataset, aes(x = factor(station), y = var)) +
   geom_bar(stat = "identity", col = "black", fill = "white") +
   facet_grid(. ~ area, scales = "free_x", space = "free") +
   labs(x= "station")

The "free_x" argument allows for varying numbers of levels per facet;
the space = "free" argument resizes the space proportionally in each
facet to the number of available levels.

As far as the labels are concerned, your request is possible but
requires some surgery with the grid and gtable packages. The
suggestion to facet by area is simpler and accomplishes the same
purpose.

An alternative to this is a Cleveland dot chart. I prefer the way it's
done in base graphics, where spacing is used to separate groups rather
than faceting. A basic version would be

with(dataset, dotchart(var, labels = station, groups = area, pch = 16))

Dennis

messages.subject: passing variables to coord_map
messages.body_plain:
Hi ggplot devs/users,

I have been using ggplot to make maps using the `coord_map` function. I am writing a custom mapping function that wraps `coord_map` and I would like some suggestions on how to pass parameters to it.

The basic problem is that coord_map <http://docs.ggplot2.org/current/coord_map.html> calls another function, mapproj <http://www.inside-r.org/packages/cran/mapproj/docs/mapproject>, that handles the projections. The different projections require different parameters: some projections don't need any additional parameters, some need two (lat0=10,lat1=50) and so on.   The `coord_map` function does NOT specify these parameters and I would like to copy this style as closely as possible. It seems to me the alternative is to specify ALL possible parameters and then dispatch the function on a case-by-case basis using the relevant additional parameters. This second way would pollute the funciton argument namespace with parameters that won't be used most of the time.

So what I would like to do is something like the following where I can "pass the values through" to `coord_map`.  I know this is generally frowned upon as explicit better than implicit but it seems there is a case to be made for it here. I  would appreciate your suggestions on how to do this or some other way to achieve the same result.

```[R]
wrap_map <- function(gplot, ..., projection="",orientation=NULL){
    gmap + coord_map(...)
}

# these should both work
warp_map(gplot,projection="mercator")
wrap_map(gplot, projection="conic", lat0 = 30)
```

thanks,
zach cp

On 27 January 2015 at 22:21, Dennis Murphy <djm...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hi:
>
> Here are a couple of suggestions. I think the first is what you were after.
>
> library(ggplot2)
> ggplot(dataset, aes(x = factor(station), y = var)) +
>    geom_bar(stat = "identity", col = "black", fill = "white") +
>    facet_grid(. ~ area, scales = "free_x", space = "free") +
>    labs(x= "station")
>
> The "free_x" argument allows for varying numbers of levels per facet;
> the space = "free" argument resizes the space proportionally in each
> facet to the number of available levels.
>
> As far as the labels are concerned, your request is possible but
> requires some surgery with the grid and gtable packages. The
> suggestion to facet by area is simpler and accomplishes the same
> purpose.
>
> An alternative to this is a Cleveland dot chart. I prefer the way it's
> done in base graphics, where spacing is used to separate groups rather
> than faceting. A basic version would be
>
> with(dataset, dotchart(var, labels = station, groups = area, pch = 16))
>
> Dennis
>
> On Tue, Jan 27, 2015 at 5:20 AM, Ellen Pape <ellen...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Hi all,
> >
> > I have the following (imaginary) dataset
> >
> > area<-c(rep("A",2),rep("B",5),rep("C",3))
> > area
> > station<-c(1:2,1:5,1:3)
> > station
> > var<-c(5.4,4.8,4.4,5.2,3.3,4.2,4.1,6.2,5.1,5.0)
> > dataset<-data.frame(area,station,var)
> >
> > in every area (A,B,C) a variable (var) is measured in several stations. The
> > number of stations varies between these areas.
> > I want to make a barplot, with a bar per station grouped per area. This is
> > the code I used:
> >
> > library(ggplot2)
> > plot<-ggplot(dataset, aes(x=area,
> > y=var,group=station))+geom_bar(width=0.5,colour="black",fill="white",stat="identity",position=position_dodge(width=0.6),drop=F)+scale_y_continuous("Sediment
> > depth averaged TOM (%)\n",limits=c(0,8),expand=c(0,0))+scale_x_discrete("")
> > plot
> >
> > This is nice but the width of the bars varies per area since the number of
> > stations investigated per area is different, i.e. the more stations in an
> > area, the narrower the bars.
> >
> > So, I would like to make the following adjustments:
> >
> > - I want to have a fixed bar width regardless of the number of stations in
> > each area
> > - For the labels on the x axis, I would like to have the stations first, and
> > below the area
> >
> > Can someone help me?
> >
> > Thanks!
> > ellen
